title: Suffix Arrays and Suffix Trees (Intro)
summary: A suffix array sorts every suffix of a string to answer substring questions fast. Learn what it stores, how it's built, the LCP array's role, and why interviews expect recognition of the technique, not a from-scratch build.

slides.markdown:
A **suffix array** takes every suffix of a string — n of them, for a string of length n — and sorts them lexicographically, storing only their **starting indices** in that sorted order. That one structure, plus a companion array of longest-common-prefixes between adjacent suffixes, unlocks a surprising amount: pattern search in O(m log n), the longest repeated substring, and (with more work) the longest common substring between two strings.

This topic covers the structure at an intro level: what it stores, the complexity of building it, binary-searching it, and the LCP array — not a full from-scratch O(n log n) construction, which is rarely expected to be reproduced live in an interview.

For `s = "banana"`, the suffixes are `"banana"`, `"anana"`, `"nana"`, `"ana"`, `"na"`, `"a"` — starting at indices 0 through 5. Sort those strings alphabetically: `"a"`, `"ana"`, `"anana"`, `"banana"`, `"na"`, `"nana"`. The suffix array is just the **starting indices** in that sorted order: `[5, 3, 1, 0, 4, 2]`.

Critically, the array does not store the suffix strings themselves — reconstructing any suffix is just `s[index:]`. This is the same space discipline a suffix array shares with a good index: store just enough to reconstruct anything, not the data itself duplicated.

slides.markdown:
![Suffix array indices for banana in one column and the actual suffix strings in the other, visibly in alphabetical order](assets/suffix-array-sorted-suffixes.svg)

The picture makes the definition concrete: reading down the right column gives alphabetical order, and the left column is simply "where did this suffix start in the original string" — that's the entire content of a suffix array.

assets.alt: Suffix array indices for banana in one column and the actual suffix strings in the other, visibly in alphabetical order

slides.markdown:
The naive build: generate all n suffixes, sort them with a standard comparison sort. Each comparison between two suffixes can itself cost O(n) in the worst case (comparing character by character), so naive construction costs **O(n² log n)** — comparison sort's O(n log n) comparisons, each up to O(n).

**Prefix doubling** gets this to **O(n log n)** total. The idea: first rank every suffix by its first 1 character, then re-rank by its first 2 characters (reusing the 1-character ranks to compare in O(1) instead of O(2)), then first 4, then first 8 — doubling the compared prefix length each round. After ⌈log₂ n⌉ rounds the compared prefix covers the whole string, and each round's re-ranking is a single O(n log n) sort using the previous round's ranks as an O(1) comparison key.

The **LCP array** adds one more piece of information on top of the suffix array: `LCP[i]` is the length of the longest common prefix between the suffix at sorted position `i` and the suffix at sorted position `i-1` — i.e., between adjacent entries once sorted.

Why adjacent, specifically: sorting groups similar suffixes together, so the longest common prefix between *any* two suffixes in the sorted order is always achieved by some pair of *adjacent* suffixes in between them (a standard property of sorted strings) — so you never need to compare non-adjacent pairs to answer common-prefix questions across the whole array.

The longest repeated substring in `s` is simply the **maximum value in the LCP array**. Two suffixes with a long shared prefix mean that prefix appears at two different starting positions in `s` — which is exactly the definition of a repeated substring — and sorting places the suffixes with the longest shared prefixes adjacent to each other, so the LCP array's maximum captures it directly.

For `s = "banana"`, the LCP array (aligned to the sorted suffix order `a, ana, anana, banana, na, nana`) peaks at 3, between `"ana"` and `"anana"` — and indeed `"ana"` repeats in `"banana"` (positions 1 and 3).

| | Suffix array | Suffix tree |
|---|---|---|
| What it stores | Sorted suffix start indices (an array) | Every suffix as a root-to-leaf path, shared prefixes merged into one path (a tree, like a trie over all suffixes) |
| Memory | O(n) integers — compact | O(n) nodes, but with real pointer overhead per node |
| Pattern search | O(m log n) via binary search (+ LCP tricks push this to O(m + log n)) | O(m) — walk the tree directly |
| Construction | O(n log n) (prefix doubling) or O(n) (advanced algorithms) | O(n) with advanced algorithms (Ukkonen's), non-trivial to implement |
| Practical use | The default choice — simpler, cache-friendlier | Used when O(m) search matters more than build/memory cost |

A suffix array trades a small amount of search-time elegance for a much simpler, more compact representation — which is why it's the one that shows up in practice and in interviews, while suffix trees are more often discussed conceptually than implemented from scratch.

Treating a from-scratch O(n log n) suffix array construction as something you're expected to derive live in an interview is a miscalibration. Most interviews that touch suffix arrays expect you to **recognize** the structure — know what it stores, what it makes fast, and roughly how prefix doubling gets to O(n log n) — not to implement prefix doubling correctly under time pressure, which is genuinely fiddly (rank comparisons, tie-breaking, radix-sort optimizations for the true O(n) versions).

The practically useful skill: know when a problem is suffix-array-shaped ("longest repeated substring," "k-th smallest suffix," "longest common substring of two strings") and be able to describe the approach and its complexity — reaching for a library implementation or a simpler O(n² log n) sort-based build when actual code is required, unless the interviewer explicitly wants the optimized construction.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this sits in the toolkit
slides.markdown: Suffix arrays close out the "sort or hash every substring/suffix" family that started with tries, KMP, Rabin-Karp, and the Z-array. What's different here: those four all answer questions about *one* pattern against *one* text. Suffix structures answer questions about a string's relationship to **all of its own substrings at once** — repeats, k-th smallest suffix, common substrings across two texts — which is why they show up specifically when a problem's phrasing involves "every substring" or "any two positions," rather than a single fixed pattern.
